outputs.L1:
Mother, the root of this little yellow flower  
Among the stones has the taste of quinine.  
Things are strange today on the cliff. The sun shines so brightly,  
And the grasshopper works so hard  
At his sewing machine.  
Here’s one on my hand, Mother—look;  
I lie so still. There’s one on your book.

But I have something stranger to tell. So leave  
Your book to the grasshopper, Mother dear—  
Like a green knight in a dazzling marketplace—  
And listen now. Can you hear what I hear  
Far out? Now and then, the foam there curls  
And stretches out a white arm like a girl’s.

Fishes and gulls ring no bells. There cannot be  
A chapel or church between here and Devon,  
With fishes or gulls ringing its bell—hark!—  
Somewhere beneath the sea or up in heaven.

“It’s the bell, my son, out in the bay,  
Upon the buoy. It does sound sweet today.”

Sweeter I have never heard, Mother—no, not in all Wales.  
I should like to lie beneath that foam,  
Dead, yet able to hear the sound of the bell,  
And certain that you would often come  
And rest there, listening happily.  
I should be happy if that could be.
outputs.L2:
Mother, the tiny yellow blossom growing through the rocks  
Has a root as bitter as quinine.  
Everything on the cliff feels unusual today. The sunlight blazes,  
And the grasshopper busily rattles like a sewing machine.  
Look, Mother—one has settled on my hand  
While I remain perfectly still, and another rests upon your book.  

Yet I must tell you of something stranger.  
Let the grasshopper have your book, dear Mother—  
He resembles a green knight standing in a brilliant marketplace—  
And listen closely. Do you hear that distant sound?  
From time to time, the sea foam bends  
And reaches out a pale arm, like a young woman.  

Neither fish nor seabirds can ring bells,  
And surely no church or chapel lies between this cliff and Devon  
Where gulls or fishes could pull a bell rope. Listen!  
The ringing must come from beneath the waves  
Or from somewhere high in heaven.  

“My son, that is the buoy’s bell  
Out in the bay. Today its music is especially lovely.”  

Mother, I have never heard anything sweeter,  
Not anywhere in Wales. I wish I could lie beneath that foam,  
Dead, yet still capable of hearing the bell,  
Knowing you would often visit  
And sit there, peacefully listening.  
If that were possible, I would be content.
outputs.L3:
On a sunny cliff above the sea, a child gazes closely at the vivid natural world around him. He notices a yellow flower with a bitter root and watches the grasshoppers moving busily through the warm grass. Everything seems bright, alive, and full of mystery.

Suddenly, he hears the distant sound of a bell. He asks his mother to put down her book and listen. The ringing appears to come from far across the water, and the child wonders where such a strange bell could be. Perhaps, he imagines, it belongs to a church hidden beneath the sea, or perhaps to a church in heaven. Yet he knows that neither the fish below nor the gulls overhead could be ringing it.

His mother explains that the sound comes from a buoy floating in the bay. She listens too and remarks on how sweetly its bell carries over the water.

The sound fills the child with a solemn, dreamlike longing. He imagines lying dead beneath the white foam of the sea, still able to hear the buoy’s gentle bell. In this fantasy, he would not feel lonely or afraid, because his mother would come often to visit him, and the distant ringing would continue to comfort him.
outputs.L4:
The child stood with his mother on the high, sunlit cliff. Below them the sea stretched away in sheets of blue and silver, breaking against the rocks in long white folds of foam. Gulls wheeled in the warm air, and the wind carried the sharp scent of salt and wild grass.

Far out upon the water, a buoy rose and dipped with the waves. Each time it swayed, its bell gave a faint, solemn note.

The child listened.

“Where is that bell?” he asked. “Is it ringing under the sea?”

His mother shaded her eyes and looked toward the small dark shape among the glittering waves.

“No,” she said. “It is hanging upon the buoy.”

But the child continued to listen, his imagination following the sound beyond anything he could see.

“Perhaps it is beneath the water,” he said, “where the drowned sailors lie. Perhaps they hear it ringing over them.”

A wave struck the cliff below, and for a moment the bell was lost in the rush and thunder of the foam. Then its voice returned, distant and clear.

“Or perhaps,” the child said, “it is not in the sea at all. Perhaps it is high in heaven, and we only hear it because the sky is so bright today.”

His mother smiled and drew him closer. Together they stood in the sunshine while the bell sounded again and again, seeming now to rise from the deep and now to fall from the immense blue air.

The child watched the foam gather over the rocks. It looked soft from that height, like white blankets laid upon the water.

“When I am dead,” he said quietly, “I should like to lie down there beneath the foam.”

His mother’s hand tightened around his.

“You must not wish for that.”

“I would not be lonely,” he answered. “The bell would ring above me. The fish would pass by, and the waves would cover me with white flowers.”

He turned to her with a grave, tender expression.

“And you would come to the cliff to visit me. You would stand here in the sunlight and listen. Whenever the bell rang, you would know that I was still near you.”

For a moment his mother said nothing. The sea shone before them, beautiful and immeasurable, while the buoy bent to every passing wave. Its bell gave another lonely note.

Then she knelt and embraced him.

“I would always listen for you,” she whispered. “But I would rather hear your living voice beside me.”

The child rested against her, looking out over the water. The thought of death passed from him as lightly as a cloud crossing the sun. Yet the bell continued to ring in the distance, joining sea and sky, sorrow and beauty, the child’s dreaming heart and his mother’s enduring love.
outputs.L5:
### The Things Mother Kept

Mother kept the things everyone else had forgotten: a chipped blue cup, a bundle of letters tied with ribbon, the tiny shoes we had outgrown. To us, they were ordinary objects. To her, each one held a voice, a face, or a moment that could not be replaced.

“The smallest things often carry the greatest memories,” Mother would say.

Years later, when the house grew quiet, we opened her old wooden box. Inside, beneath the photographs and faded notes, we found a message in her handwriting:

*Keep what reminds you to love.*

Only then did we understand why Mother had saved all those things.
